messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Marcus was sixty-eight years old, a former professional dancer who still taught a weekly master class at a community studio in Brooklyn. He had been widowed for twelve years, and dance had been his steady companion ever since. The accident happened on a rainy November evening, after a rehearsal. He was driving home through an intersection when a delivery truck ran a red light and slammed into the driver’s side of his sedan. The impact pinned him against the steering wheel; his right hip shattered, three ribs cracked, and the steering column crushed his left foot—his dancer’s foot. He remembers the shriek of metal, the taste of blood, the smell of gasoline, but beyond that the memory frays. He cannot tell a clear story of what happened, even to himself. When he tries to deliberately remember, the images slip away like water through his fingers, leaving only a sense of confusion and a hollow dread. He has fragments—the truck looming sideways, glass exploding, a paramedic’s face asking if he could feel his legs—but no coherent thread. That fractured quality has come to feel like a personal failing, as though his own mind has betrayed him. That very conviction—that his mind had betrayed him—made the memory even more slippery each time he tried to pin it down, as if his own judgment were actively shredding the few threads he had left.

In the months after the accident, Marcus began to notice that he could no longer trust his body. The hip healed, the foot recovered enough for him to walk without a cane, but a deep sense of unreliability had settled in. He started to doubt his own judgment, too—whether he had checked both ways before entering the intersection, whether he had misjudged the truck’s speed, whether he could ever make a safe decision again. And he grew angry at the traffic light that had malfunctioned that night, at the city that had not fixed it, at the hospital that had taken thirty minutes to extract him. The people and institutions that should have protected him had let him down, and that knowledge burrowed into him like a splinter he could not remove.

Because he could not trust his own body or his choices, Marcus began to avoid going out at all. He stopped driving entirely. He cancelled his master class for three months, then started again only after the studio director insisted, but he arranged to teach alone in the empty studio, never at the same time as other classes. Seeing the dancers he had socialised with before the accident—people he had known for decades, whose faces and laughter were woven into his life—became unbearable. He was certain they would ask about the accident, or worse, they would see the hesitation in his step and know he was no longer the dancer he had been. So he stopped returning calls, stopped attending the informal gatherings after class, stopped showing up at the annual showcase. His phone rang less and less. He noticed but told himself it was better this way.

When he did leave the apartment, Marcus felt unsafe unless his back was against a wall, with the entire room in front of him visible. Any unexpected or loud sound—a car horn, a truck braking, a door slamming in the hallway—sent a jolt through his chest. He was convinced something bad was about to happen. When the subway was delayed, he assumed a crash or a shooting, not a signal problem. That hypervigilance fed back into his avoidance: the more on edge he felt in public, the less he wanted to go out, and the less he went out, the more unfamiliar and threatening the world became. His therapist, whom he had started seeing six months after the accident, encouraged him to talk about the collision. But Marcus found that whenever the therapist asked him to describe the moment of impact, his mind went blank. He could not hold onto the sequence. That blankness only deepened his conviction that his memory was unreliable, which in turn made him more vigilant for the missing pieces, which made him avoid the therapy content altogether. He stopped attending sessions after the fourth appointment, telling himself he would go back when he felt ready—a readiness that never came.

What finally brought Marcus to seek help again was a small incident that felt enormous. Last week, while teaching a plié combination, a dancer dropped a metal water bottle on the hardwood floor. The clatter was sharp and sudden. Marcus spun around, dropped into a defensive crouch, and then stood frozen, his heart hammering, his students staring. He could not finish the class. He walked out, ashamed and terrified that his body had betrayed him once more, this time in front of the very people he had been avoiding. Now he sits in a new therapist’s office, not sure what he hopes for, but certain of what he fears: that the fracture inside him will never fully heal, that he will never trust his own body or his own mind again, and that dance—the one thing that has anchored him since his wife died—will slip away as well.
